 Kokoyo Nyonya Delights Closing After $50K Losses; Hawker, 25, Will Open The Porridge Stall Instead
 “It’s quite a pity, it’s like I failed. But I gave it my best shot,” says the hawker, who opened Kokoyo to honour his Peranakan granny’s recipes.

 Kokoyo Nyonya Delights, a stall selling Peranakan food including blue pea nasi lemak , ayam buah keluak and beef rendang, is closing after two years in business. Its last day at Hougang Mall’s fourth-floor food court is on November 2.
Co-owner Ernest Ang, 25, tells 8days.sg that the business has accumulated an estimated $50,000 in losses since February this year. Sales have also fallen by about half, with business becoming particularly difficult since September.
 No part of this story or photos can be reproduced without permission from 8days.sg . 
 1 of 8 
 Kokoyo’s nasi lemak features blue pea coconut rice.
Photo: Kokoyo Nyonya Delights
 While the Kokoyo brand is closing for good, Ernest and his brother, co-owner Irwin Ang, 29, are staying put. They plan to launch a seafood porridge concept at the same space called The Porridge Stall. The siblings hope this comforting dish will help turn things around.
 2 of 8 
 Kokoyo’s Hougang Mall stall.
Photo: Kokoyo Nyonya Delights
 $11K monthly rent; sales down by half 
 The brothers announced Kokoyo’s closure in a video posted on the brand’s Instagram page on Oct 21.
They explained that footfall at the food court was initially healthy when there were fewer dining options elsewhere in Hougang Mall. Following renovations and the arrival of more eateries on other floors, they found it increasingly difficult to draw customers up to the fourth floor.
“It’s been rough these past few months, foot traffic to the food court has dropped drastically compared to when we first entered,” says Ernest.
With monthly rent of $11,000, the drop in sales has been difficult to sustain.
“The rent is high, so the breakeven point is high,” Ernest tells 8days.sg . “There has to be a benchmark we need to hit every day, but then the footfall is not good, so it’s directly related.”
Kokoyo first opened as a standalone eatery in Serangoon Central in 2024, before relocating to Jelita Mall as a food court stall in Holland Road, then Hougang Mall in February this year. Ernest says the business had already begun incurring losses at Jelita Mall, and earlier earnings have gone towards covering those losses.
So why take another risk at Hougang Mall? Ernest, who lives in Hougang, says he was initially confident about customer traffic there. He estimates that food establishments made up only about 30 per cent of the mall when Kokoyo moved in.
What he hadn’t anticipated was the extent of the mall’s refurbishment under an asset enhancement initiative. As more eateries gradually opened, competition for diners increased.
 3 of 8 
 Ernest with his granny back in 2024, whose Peranakan recipes inspired Kokoyo.
Photo: Kelvin Chia
 Started with $80K capital and granny’s closely guarded recipes 
 When 8days.sg first featured Ernest in 2024 , he was a fresh electronics engineering diploma holder who had stopped job hunting after six weeks to open his own eatery.
His grandmother contributed $40,000 — half the initial investment — while Ernest funded the rest with savings from part-time jobs. She also taught him her closely guarded Peranakan recipes, tasting and approving dishes before they went on the menu.
Her involvement extended beyond sharing recipes: when Kokoyo first opened, she made around 200 pieces of nonya kueh daily from home for the eatery. Ernest shares that she has since stopped supplying them due to mobility issues.
Even the brand’s name was a tribute to her: Kokoyo came from the way she pronounced “coconut”, while the cartoon logo was also modelled after her.
 4 of 8 
 Kokoyo co-owners and bros Irwin (left), 29, and Ernest Ang, 25.
Photo: Instagram/kokoyosg
 Although our earlier feature focused on Ernest, he clarifies that his older brother Irwin, who has a degree in marketing, has been involved in the business since the start. Hougang Mall is their only remaining outlet, and the brothers work at the stall daily.
 5 of 8 
 Ernest, then 23, at Kokoyo’s now-defunct Serangoon Central eatery.
Photo: Kelvin Chia
 “It’s quite a pity lah” 
 For Ernest, giving up the brand means letting go of a business he started to honour his grandmother’s cooking.
“It’s quite a pity lah. It’s like I failed, but I gave it my best shot, so that’s all that matters,” he shares.
His grandmother has taken the decision in her stride. According to Ernest, she feels that if the business isn’t working, they should “stop the bleeding”.
 6 of 8 
 Kokoyo’s offerings include ayam buah keluak, spiced fried chicken, fried pork belly and beef rendang.
Photo: Kokoyo Nyonya Delights
 Nasi lemak sets from $4.90 
 For those hoping to visit before the closure, Kokoyo’s current menu centres on blue pea nasi lemak. Its Nasi Lemak Kosong ($4.90) comes with a fried egg, ikan bilis, peanuts, cucumber, achar and sambal.
Other options include the Inchi Kabin Berempah Set ($7.50) , featuring spiced fried chicken, and Ayam Buah Keluak Set ($7.50) . There’s also a Fried Pork Belly Set ($8.50) and Beef Rendang Nasi Lemak ($11.50) , featuring beef slow-cooked in a spiced coconut gravy.
À la carte dishes include Homemade Ngoh Hiang ($5.80) and Nyonya Chap Chye (from $4.80) , while sharing sets for two start at $20.50.
 7 of 8 
 Beef rendang.
Photo: Kelvin Chia
 Replacing the Peranakan menu with seafood porridge 
 The Porridge Stall will take over the space after Kokoyo closes. Staying at the same spot is a practical decision — their existing lease runs until February 2027.
He settled on seafood porridge after visiting eateries in Malaysia in search of a new concept. He describes his version as Guangdong-style porridge, with a consistency somewhere between thick Cantonese congee and the looser Teochew style.
The base will be a broth made with chicken and pork bones. The opening date has yet to be confirmed.
 8 of 8 
 Inchi kabin berempah (spiced fried chicken).
Photo: Kelvin Chia
 “It’s worth a gamble” 
 Ernest hopes the switch will help the brothers reach a wider customer base.
“I just want to go for a very mass market dish. I don’t want to go for something very niche like nonya food anymore,” he says. “I believe for many people in Singapore, porridge has a childhood connection.”
He also sees a gap in the mall’s food offerings. According to him, there are four nasi lemak sellers, including Kokoyo, but no dedicated porridge stall.
“I feel the success rate will be higher, and I think it’s worth a gamble rather than not doing anything about it,” he says.
If the new concept does well, the brothers are open to continuing the biz beyond their current stall’s lease.
 Why he prefers not to get a corporate job 
 Would Ernest consider getting a corporate job if things don’t work out? “I will study the numbers and make a decision,” he muses. For now, he prefers to stay in F&B and may try his luck at another location.
Why stick with a notoriously punishing industry that hasn’t been kind to him? “I feel like this shouldn’t be the end of my journey. I’m not the type of person that gives up easily,” he reasons.
He adds that building a brand is something both he and his brother enjoy.
And what do his dad, a technician, and mum, who works in HR, think of their sons’ rocky F&B ventures? “My parents are pretty chill about it [despite our losses],” says Ernest simply.
 Kokoyo Nyonya Delights’ last day of operation is on 2 Nov. #04-11 Hougang Mall, 90 Hougang Ave 10, S538766. Open Mon–Fri, 11.30am–8pm; Sat & Sun, 11am–8pm. More info via Instagram .
